title: Denver approves $40M of ‘standby’ funding for Democratic National Convention
summary: The city will provide a financial guarantee for the DNC bid.
content: Denver will provide a $40 million reimbursable grant for the effort to bring the Democratic National Convention to Colorado in 2028. The Denver City Council voted 9-2 Monday night to approve the “standby” funding for the city’s bid to host the nominating convention. Councilmember Stacie Gilmore voted no, saying she didn’t trust the mayor’s administration. Councilmember Shontel Lewis also voted no. City leaders stress the money is not expected to fund the convention itself. Instead, the grant to the Denver 2028 Host Committee is supposed to be a backup — it will only be spent if Denver is selected for the convention and private fundraising falls short. “We don’t anticipate these funds being used,” said Dawnna Wilder, a senior project manager in Denver’s finance department, during Monday’s meeting. Denver is one of the three finalists for the convention, alongside Boston and Philadelphia. The DNC is held every four years to nominate the party’s presidential candidate and rally Democrats from across the country ahead of the election. The convention will be Aug. 7-10, 2028. Councilmember Darrell Watson called setting the funds aside a good use of DDDA funding. “I think having the opportunity to actually lead the Democratic National Convention here in Denver is something that we cannot miss,” Watson said. What’s the money for? Mayor Mike Johnston said in an interview that the money won’t actually be spent on the convention. “The DNC requires you to put up a guarantee that you’ll raise the money to host the event,” Johnston said. “This is just a guarantee against those dollars. So they’re not spent.” An agreement for the grant described the funding as “standby in nature,” noting it is “not a contribution to the operating budget of the Host Committee or the (Democratic National Convention Committee).” The DNCC requires that host cities “demonstrate that a standby source of funds is immediately available to cover any shortfall in that fundraising commitment,” the grant agreement states. The money could only be spent if “the Host Committee’s private fundraising falls short of specified benchmarks,” according to the agreement; the city and the local bid committee both “expect” that the grant will be returned untouched to the Denver Downtown Development Authority. If any money is spent, the committee would be obligated to repay it; no interest would be assessed until 2029. The DDDA, which collects a portion of downtown taxes, is putting up the money for the guarantee. “And so we think that’s a great use of the DDDA dollars because they’re focused on activating downtown. This would be the most epic activation of downtown in 20 years probably,” Johnston said. Voters in 2024 approved a package of more than $500 million of DDDA spending. Records show city leaders also expect to add the Colorado Convention Center and some downtown hotels into the district’s borders, allowing them to receive DDDA funding. Protection proclamation voted in Councilmembers Serena Gonzales-Gutierrez and Jamie Torres introduced a proclamation made up of five essential conditions to help protect residents should Denver be chosen for the conference. Included were protections for peaceful protests, no conference-related encampment sweeps and no excessive use of force. The proclamation passed unanimously. “If Denver were awarded the opportunity to host the 2028 DNC, it would bring national attention, large crowds and significant public safety operations to our city to ensure the safety of all guests and attendees,” Gonzales-Gutierrez said during Monday’s meeting. “Protections should be planned well in advance. All residents, whether they are housed or unhoused, are entitled to safety, dignity and the protection of their persons and property.” Johnston’s campaigning for the DNC The mayor has been busy trying to convince the committee to select Denver. Earlier this month, the city hosted hundreds of leaders and members of the national Democratic Party as it tries to game plan and capitalize on the blue tsunami out of the midterms. Denver also hosted national party chair Ken Martin and other top officials in May . “In 2028, Democrats will gather at the national convention to reaffirm the core principles of our party and nominate the next president of the United States of America,” Martin said at a press conference in May. “We are grateful to Denver for its interest in hosting this historic moment. Hosting a national convention, of course, can be a great economic boom for any city.” Denver last hosted the DNC in 2008, when then-candidate Barack Obama accepted the party’s presidential nomination. Obama’s campaign centered on “hope,” a theme Johnston thinks will resonate today. “This city and the ‘08 convention made famous the idea of hope and change,” Johnston said in May. “As we think about this coming convention, it is true that often hope inspires change, but it is more profoundly true that change drives hope. And what fundamentally Americans want to see right now is that we find ourselves the most frustrated when you expect something to get fixed and it doesn’t.” One critique from the 2008 conference was the treatment of unhoused people before and during the event. “We can’t forget how things went down in 2008. How thousands of unhoused people in Denver were swept away so that visitors did not see the housing crisis that we were experiencing,” Lewis said during Monday’s meeting. “This should be met with humanity. I’m really hopeful that the mayor’s administration does what is asked in this proclamation so that we can learn from our past and not make those mistakes again.” City projections estimate the convention would bring a broader economic impact of approximately $226.3 million, a boost of approximately $7.2 million to local tax revenues, and approximately 1,112 temporary jobs.

title: Sorry, those Saturday flurries didn’t count as Denver’s official first snow
summary: We're already looking at the third-latest snow on record.
content: Denverites woke up to the welcome sight of snowfall on Saturday, but it was too light to qualify as the first snow of the year, according to the National Weather Service. Denver International Airport, where the NWS takes its official measurements for the city, recorded about 20 minutes of extremely light snow on Saturday morning. “That’ll go down as a trace, meaning that it wasn’t a measurable snow, and so we’re still kind of waiting on that right now,” said Zach Hiris, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service. Last year, Denver’s first snowfall came on Nov. 29, the city’s second-latest on record. The record was Dec. 10 in 2021. This year is already set to be the third-latest snowfall or worse. The wait is expected to continue, with Hiris saying there’s no significant promise of snow for Denver on the horizon. Other parts of the Front Range are picking up more accumulation. Some parts of the foothills got 4 to 7 inches of snow. A few more storms are tracking toward the state in the coming days, and the weather pattern through mid-December is favorable for snow, OpenSnow reported , though the northern mountains still don’t have a base. Last year was one of Denver’s roughest on record. The city saw a mere 13.4 inches of snowfall between September and February .

title: Denver is in the mix to host games for the 2031 Women’s World Cup
summary: The Women’s World Cup is coming to the United States, Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica.
content: Denver has a second shot to host FIFA World Cup games. FIFA, the governing body for global football ( or soccer, for us Americans ), announced Monday that it had awarded the 2031 Women’s World Cup to the United States, Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica . The joint bid lists 14 cities that could host games in the United States. Denver is among the suitors with Empower Field at Mile High. If Denver is selected, it could leave a lasting footprint in the city. Official documents say that “the city will convert World Cup infrastructure, including mini-pitches and modular facilities, into permanent community assets in underserved neighborhoods.” “Denver views the FIFA Women’s World Cup 2031 as a catalyst for lasting change,” the bid book reads . “By investing in inclusive infrastructure, supporting grassroots development, and celebrating the power of sport to unite communities, Denver will not only host the world but inspire it.” The men’s version of the competition was just in the United States for the 2026 World Cup. But Denver was not among the cities hosting, with FIFA denying the city’s bid to host games back in 2022. But Denver has come a long way in soccer culture. In the years since, Denver has seen the launch of Denver Summit FC, the city’s first professional women’s sports team. The Summit, which recently ended its inaugural season without making the playoffs, is currently building its permanent stadium in Denver’s Baker neighborhood , where it hopes to play in 2028. What Empower Field at Mile High will look like in 2031 is in flux. The Denver Broncos hope to move into a new stadium for the 2031 season , which is expected to start after the Women’s World Cup. The United States hosted the Women’s World Cup in 1999 and 2003. Denver was also not a part of those tournaments. Many of the American cities included in the joint bid were chosen for 2026 World Cup games, meaning Denver continues to face stiff competition from its national peers. But the host cities won’t be announced for some time. “Additional details regarding host cities, stadiums, match schedules, ticketing and tournament operations will be announced in coordination with FIFA and the participating host federations as planning progresses,” a U.S. Soccer press release said. The full list of U.S. cities in the running are: Atlanta Charlotte Dallas Denver Houston Kansas City Los Angeles Minneapolis Nashville New York/New Jersey Orlando San Diego Seattle Washington, D.C.
